slides.title: From videos to a moving 3D scene
bullets: Goal: replay a skate trick from a new viewpoint.
Part 1: how the reconstruction works.
Part 2: data acquisition and actual results.
slides.notes: The goal of my project is to reconstruct a moving 3D scene from videos, so that I can choose a new viewpoint and a moment in the replay. I will first explain the reconstruction process, step by step. Then I will present the data acquisition and compare the kitchen reference scene with my own True Skate recordings.

slides.title: Step 1 — prepare images of the same moment
bullets: Extract frames from each camera view.
Align the moments represented by the frames.
Keep image size and camera parameters consistent.
slides.notes: The first step is to turn the videos into image sequences. At each training instant, the views should show the same state of the scene. Otherwise, the model receives conflicting observations. Image resizing must also be reflected in the camera parameters. In the project, FFmpeg extracts the frames and Python prepares the dataset. This requires consistent sampling and image coordinates. Later, I will explain how I acquired the actual recordings.

slides.title: Step 2 — recover the cameras and 3D points
bullets: Find the same background details in several images.
Estimate camera poses and triangulate 3D points.
Check that the points project back to the right pixels.
slides.notes: The reconstruction needs the position and orientation of each camera, as well as its projection parameters. If these are not supplied, COLMAP estimates them from matching details in the static background. It estimates camera poses and triangulates sparse 3D points, then refines them together. Reprojection checks compare predicted pixels with observed pixels. Coordinate transformations and perspective connect the 3D points to image pixels. For the kitchen dataset, calibrated cameras are supplied; for True Skate, I estimate them.

slides.title: From a 3D point to an image pixel
bullets: Transform the point into the camera coordinate system.
Divide by depth and apply the camera intrinsics.
Check visibility before using the projected point.
slides.notes: The camera pose transforms a world point into camera coordinates. Perspective projection divides its horizontal and vertical coordinates by depth, then applies the focal length and image center. The function project performs this calculation and returns depth as well as pixels. Visibility must be checked separately. In our project, a near-plane mismatch initially removed board seeds. The function require_board_visibility now rejects unsafe initial seeds. This connects coordinate transformations, perspective and clipping.

slides.title: What is a 3D Gaussian?
bullets: A soft 3D ellipsoid with a center, size and orientation.
Opacity controls its contribution; appearance controls color.
Many overlapping elements represent the scene.
slides.notes: A three-dimensional Gaussian is a soft ellipsoid, with influence strongest near its center and decreasing away from it. Its parameters describe its position, size along several axes, orientation, opacity and appearance. The scene is represented by many overlapping elements. Their two-dimensional projected footprints look like soft ellipses; the drawing here is schematic. GaussianModel.create_from_pcd initializes these elements from a point cloud. The scene starts as an approximation: a seed is not necessarily an accurate point on the board surface. Density control can split elements to represent more detail.

slides.title: How do Gaussians produce and learn an image?
bullets: Project the elements and combine their contributions by depth and opacity.
Compare the rendered image with the recorded target.
Use gradients to update scene parameters, then repeat.
slides.notes: For a chosen camera, the renderer projects the Gaussians into the image and combines their contributions in depth order using opacity. This produces pixels. Rendering alone does not improve the model. During training, the rendered image is compared with a recorded target. The difference becomes a loss. PyTorch computes gradients through the renderer, and the optimizer changes the scene parameters to reduce that loss. The scene_reconstruction function manages this training loop and calls render. We repeat the process across views and times. This explains how a point-cloud initialization becomes an image-matching scene representation.

functions.label: scene_reconstruction()
functions.role: Render, compute loss and update parameters

slides.title: Step 4 — model motion and check the result
bullets: 4DGaussians predicts how the reference scene changes with time.
Dynamic 3D Gaussians fits successive states with motion constraints.
Render the scene and compare it with a reserved camera view.
slides.notes: Four-D Gaussians uses a reference scene and a network that predicts changes from time. Its forward_dynamic function predicts deformed Gaussian parameters. Dynamic Three-D Gaussians instead fits successive scene states with local motion constraints; our train adapter runs that sequence using the authors' functions. Both methods receive calibrated camera poses. This is different from training separate static reconstructions and playing them in sequence. A time-varying render is useful, but it does not automatically prove that a physical point or board rotation is tracked correctly.

slides.title: Evaluate the board, not only the background
bullets: Keep view20 out of scene optimization.
Compare full images and the moving-board region.
Inspect actual renders; high image scores can hide a missing board.
slides.notes: I reserve view20 from scene optimization and use it for validation. Its camera can be localized against the frozen background map, but its target images do not train the Gaussian scene. The probe function checks the loader, camera split and projections. The evaluation function compares saved renders with targets, including changing regions and approximate board envelopes. A high whole-image score may mainly reward the much larger background. View20 has been inspected repeatedly, so it is a reused validation camera, not a fresh final test. The latest ten times are all supervised.

slides.title: Two sources of data, two levels of control
bullets: Kitchen reference: synchronized videos and supplied calibration.
True Skate: one saved replay recorded from successive viewpoints.
Fixed views simplify calibration; timing and masks remain approximate.
slides.notes: I used two sources of data. First, I downloaded a kitchen scene from the DyNeRF reference dataset, with synchronized videos and supplied camera calibration. Second, I recorded the same saved True Skate replay from different viewpoints. I initially used following cameras, then captured fixed views to simplify pose estimation. The screen recording was split automatically and aligned using the score event. This is not a simultaneous physical camera rig. Exact replay timing, camera estimates and foreground masks still contain uncertainty.

slides.title: Kitchen reference: the pipeline works
bullets: A recognizable scene with reconstructed motion.
A small, calibrated reference experiment.
Blur and color differences remain.
slides.notes: This is the kitchen reference experiment. On the left is an input image. On the right is the actual trained model; the PowerPoint includes a three-second animation. The reconstruction is recognizable and changes with time, which confirms that the GPU pipeline can learn a dynamic scene on this calibrated input. This remains a small pilot of about one second, with blur and color errors. It is not a complete reconstruction or a physical tracking result.

slides.title: My recordings: the moving board is still difficult
slides.section: Part 2 / Own-data result and next steps
bullets: The background is recognizable, but moving-board shape is unreliable.
Separate static fits work better at selected instants.
Mask-based training was tested; it did not solve the motion problem.
slides.notes: My own recordings produce a much weaker result. The background can be recognizable, but the moving board is blurred or missing. Independent static fits worked better at selected instants, and Dynamic Three-D Gaussians also lost the board after an initial fit. The render and evaluate functions produce and inspect these outputs. We have already tested mask-based training, so the next slide explains that experiment. The kitchen and skate trials have different scenes and settings: this comparison does not isolate data quality as the sole cause.

slides.title: Masks were tested — better scores, still wrong shape
slides.section: Part 2 / Completed experiments and next steps
bullets: Candidate masks identify likely moving-object pixels.
Foreground weighting was tested and later used across multiple views.
Next: refine existing masks, timing and surface coverage.
slides.notes: We have already generated, inspected and used foreground masks in training. In an earlier controlled experiment, adding a foreground loss in view19 increased masked training PSNR from 11.79 to 25.18 decibels, but produced a broad dark smear rather than a correct skateboard. This was a training-fit improvement, not reconstruction success. Later static and temporal trials used masks across multiple views, and the latest comparison has 110 masked training images. The action_masks function builds candidates and foreground_l1 weights their RGB errors. These masks are approximate. The remaining task is to refine existing masks, verify timing and surface coverage, and validate board motion.
